name: Hot Wallet
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Hot Wallets: Convenience with a Larger Attack Surface
lesson.summary: A hot wallet keeps private keys on an internet connected device for everyday convenience, accepting a larger remote attack surface in exchange for speed.
lesson.body:
A hot wallet is any wallet whose private keys live on a device that stays connected to the internet: a mobile app, a browser extension, or the account system behind an exchange. The defining trait is connectivity, which is exactly what makes hot wallets useful for everyday activity. Sending payments, trading on an exchange, or interacting with a decentralized application all require a live connection to the network, so anyone actively using cryptocurrency day to day is, at some point, relying on a hot wallet.

That same connectivity is also the source of a hot wallet's main weakness. Everything cold storage is designed to avoid, namely a network path an attacker can use to reach the private key, is present by definition in a hot wallet. Malware on a computer or phone can scan for stored keys or intercept clipboard contents when a user copies an address. Phishing sites impersonate legitimate wallet interfaces and trick users into approving a transaction that quietly hands over funds or grants a malicious contract permission to move them later. Compromised browser extensions and fake wallet apps in app stores have been used the same way. When the wallet in question is custodial, such as the wallet inside an exchange account, an attacker does not even need to touch an individual user; compromising the exchange's own hot wallet infrastructure can expose many users' funds at once, which is what happened in some of the largest exchange hacks the industry has seen.

Because of this, the standard advice mirrors how people already handle physical cash: keep only a small operating balance in a hot wallet, enough to cover near term spending, and hold savings in cold storage instead. This is the same instinct behind carrying limited cash while keeping most of one's money in a bank vault, translated into cryptographic terms. A hot wallet compromised by malware can only lose what is actually sitting in it at that moment.

It is also worth distinguishing custodial and non-custodial hot wallets, a distinction introduced earlier when discussing wallets generally. An exchange account is a custodial hot wallet: the exchange holds the keys, and a hack of its systems is a hack of everyone's funds at once, but the exchange can also freeze suspicious activity or assist with account recovery. A browser extension wallet like a typical non-custodial mobile or desktop wallet is still hot, since it is connected to the internet, but the user alone holds the key, so a phishing attack that tricks that one user into signing a bad transaction affects only that person, with no company able to reverse it afterward.

None of this makes hot wallets a mistake to avoid entirely. They exist because some level of connectivity is unavoidable for actually using a blockchain network, not just storing value on it. The practical skill is matching the wallet to the purpose: hot for spending, cold for holding, and a clear sense of how much sits exposed on the internet connected side at any given time.
